What remains specifically distinctive about a “crime against humanity” once one subtracts the old and familiar crimes: murder, robbery, rape, and so on?
Crimes “that reveal a blatant will to annihilate.” So something additional must exist on the subjective side: something specifically anti-human.
Not a new reatus—not a new kind of criminal act.

Only a new animus: a special state of mind. These are crimes of disposition, approached from the negative side. They had to appear with dialectical necessity once crimes based on a “good” disposition had been discovered in the name of humanity.
In other words: they are acts that arise from a hostile attitude toward humanity and reveal such an attitude. That means: acts committed by someone who has been declared an enemy of humanity.
Political in the most extreme and intense meaning of the word.
“Crime against humanity” is simply the broadest possible blanket clause for destroying the enemy.
The enslavement of peasants who owed service but had until then remained free began with the transition from measured and fixed duties to unlimited duties.

Likewise, the enslavement of a population subject to the state but previously free begins with the transition from precisely defined statutory offences to so-called blanket clauses. This too belongs to the modern problem of legality.
Legality in the sense of fixed offences defined in advance, and legality in the sense of broad, undefined grants of power, are two different concepts.

Once what is unlimited enters the picture—and is therefore potentially total—the matter becomes “political” in the modern sense. That is the essence of the indictment and of criminalized offences in political trials.
The only interesting question concerns the situation itself:
Are we still capable of measuring at all?
Can we still find standards that are neither the old standards, which have become false, nor arbitrary new ones, but standards appropriate to the actual matter and the actual situation?

To a legal scholar: I have reread the good old Hall, International Law, in Higgins’s edition (8th ed., Oxford, 1924). He is old, and probably old-fashioned too, but that is exactly what makes him so instructive and so superior to positivists of the Strupp, Lauterpacht, etc. variety. His criticism of the doctrine that an occupying power exercises the sovereignty of the occupied country deserves very close attention: this would “enable to brand acts of resistance on the part of an invaded population with a stigma of criminality which is as useless as it is unjust.” Hall even has a separate chapter entitled “Postliminium.” The whole thing, in this 1924 edition, is a good example of how English jurists never experienced the break with the pre-positivist tradition that had such catastrophic consequences in Germany. I already noticed this years ago when reading Westlake.

Then there is the question of how to distinguish the theatre of war from occupied territory, especially the meaning of autorité établie—“established authority”; the difference between the executive authority of the military commander in the two cases; and the question whether, in occupied territory, this executive authority of the military commander is not itself shaped, in its organization and internal structure, by the constitutional structure of the occupying state. Here too the Hague Regulations remain at the standard of 1907, including in the relationship between military and civilian authority.

(I am deeply grateful to you simply for the possibility of talking about these things with you and telling you what is on my mind.) I am often tormented by what I call the “impatience of justice,” and it is an immense comfort to know that you understand the intention and intellectual impulse behind my way of practising legal scholarship. It matters not in the least whether, in the end, you agree or disagree with my conclusions. Your visit to Plettenberg continues to bear fruit even now, and nothing could give me greater pleasure than the further certainty that there is complete reciprocity between us in this respect. Then 21 April 1948 and 1 May 1948: Formosus, Titulus, Sallust.

Belgium, which you have come to know, has become a peculiar centre from which the destruction of the classical law of war first began. Neutrality was originally devised to guarantee security, and <…> the atomic bomb stripped that security away. You will read something in the Nomos about the genuine and great scholar Ernest Nys. But also read note 39 in my The Concept of the Discriminating War; and remember Cardinal Mercier’s Christmas pastoral letter of 1914: the legitimate authority is and remains the government of the occupied state, not the occupying power. In itself that is correct. Here, however, it was meant in a discriminatory sense and had a discriminatory effect, with the result that even the remarkable, classically developed institution of occupatio bellica—military occupation—was destroyed by it.

I came across the sentence L’initié tue l’initiateur—the initiate kills the initiator—and thought of W. Fraenger’s Grand Master of the Free Brotherhood, who was overcome by his pupil Hieronymus Bosch.
There is a mysterious cruelty in this world of initiation and mystery. The état d’esprit, the state of mind, is even crueller than Hobbes’s état de nature, the state of nature.

Here the son kills the father, the young kills the old; Zeus kills Cronus, Cronus kills Uranus. This eternal and biologically obvious process is reflected in the mysteries. They reveal, precisely by concealing it, the core of things.

Against this, Christianity, as a religion of the Father, is the true religion of peace: remaining in the Father’s house; the return of the prodigal son; the Ascension of Christ; Christ himself is the prodigal son. But there is no suggestion that the prodigal son brought some of the companions from his dissolute life back home with him. So how is the noble prodigal son supposed to take one of us back to the Father?

Let us therefore return to nature! But that means nothing other than this: let us kill our fathers, our teachers, our initiators, our creators, our benefactors. And at the same time: let us make sure that we ourselves never become fathers, teachers, initiators, creators, or benefactors!

Homo homini homo: man is man to man. That means nothing more than standing still, marking time at the zero point of a purely polar concept, which immediately splits in opposite directions: left and right, down and up; homo homini lupus or deus—man is either a wolf or a god to man.

The typical neutralization at this dead centre consists in refusing to let the split happen, or at least postponing it. One would rather stand still: on the knife-edge, right on the boundary, balanced to the finest possible degree in the transcendental space between the transcendent and the empirical; committed to nothing, keeping every option open, remaining in the undisturbed purity of the concept. But this is an untouched purity, which means an unrealized purity. It belongs to German idealism, from pure reason all the way to pure unreason.
How, then, did the fall into hell, into utter impurity, happen?
We lived through it and came to understand it.
What has happened in Germany since 1918?

Out of the darkness of social, moral, and intellectual nothingness, out of the pure lumpenproletariat, out of the refuge of homeless non-culture, rose the unknown soldier of the First World War: until then a completely empty individual, who now filled himself with the words and passions of educated Germany at that time.
H. S. Chamberlain introduced and initiated him at Wahnfried. With that, he was admitted into the temple of culture. And he took it seriously—with the seriousness of an animal.
The passions and formulas that were offered to him.

Concepts such as deed, will, power, race, genius, Führer, charisma. And conversely, these passions and formulas, which until then had been thought in a fairly pure and abstract way, were surprised and delighted that someone was finally taking them seriously.
Now there was a man who took them seriously, who made them serious: nothing but a realizer, someone to whom one could leave the rest, nothing but an executor and enforcer.
Through sheer “carrying-through,” the I comes into being—Fichte.
The pure executor of ideas that had until then remained so pure.
This individual read enormously, in order to fuel himself.
